name: Dark olive grey
lede: Dark olive grey is exactly what it says: a greyed, dark version of olive, fixed by Ridgway in 1912 with no further story behind the choice of words.

sections.title: Plain description, old source
sections.body:
This color comes from Ridgway's 1912 *Color Standards and Color Nomenclature*, plate LI, hue 23 with five primes, tone i [1]. The nearest named colors on file are [[brown-olive]], [[grey-olive]], [[greenish-umber]] and [[black-olive]], at 2.5, 2.9, 3.4 and 3.9 ΔE [1]. Ridgway also lists an alias, "Dark Olive-Grey," at a different, lighter value, #676C5C, a reminder that the same name can land on more than one plate [1].

In ISCC-NBS terms it is an olive gray, with [[greenish-umber]] and [[black-olive]] also close in our library [1].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: Our archive finds this dark olive in 2,919 of 23,781 paintings, 12.27 percent, more common than 95 percent of our named colors, as photographed [2]. It most often plays a mid-tone, in 40 percent of its appearances, with a strong secondary role as shadow [2]. Arnoud van Halen favors it most, in 17 of his 50 catalogued works, over three times the baseline for the museums those works come from [2]. The earliest dated example, from 1099, predates Ridgway's 1912 record of the name by over eight centuries, so the match is a look-alike hue in aged paint, not proof of any pigment, a floor and not a first, since the archive's early centuries are thin [2].

aka: Dark Olive-Grey (Ridgway, a separate, lighter plate value, #676C5C)
